claims.text: Increasing the number of constituents in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived alloys increases local lattice distortion.
Greater local lattice distortion elevates the friction stress opposing dislocation motion.
Elevated dislocation friction stress increases yield strength.
Elevated dislocation friction stress alters strain-hardening behavior.
Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni can retain a single-phase FCC structure after thermomechanical processing.
The corresponding quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after the same thermomechanical processing.
Variations in constituent atomic radii produce local lattice distortions.
The quinary alloy has greater lattice distortion than its ternary and quaternary subsets.
Local lattice distortions act as pinning points for dislocations.
Reduced lattice distortion in simpler subsets permits easier dislocation glide.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower yield strength than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit less dislocation pinning or entanglement than the quinary alloy.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit strain-hardening profiles different from that of the quinary alloy.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys tested at room temperature after identical thermomechanical processing.
Multiphase structures or temperature-induced changes in dislocation dynamics may invalidate the proposed relationship.
Measurement-resolution limits and overlapping defect mechanisms may obscure the quantitative relationship among lattice distortion, friction stress, and mechanical properties.
Statistically indistinguishable lattice distortion, dislocation behavior, yield strength, and strain hardening across constituent counts would falsify the proposed complexity-driven mechanism.
